**Rotating Ring Component**: An annular element is positioned to slide against the cylindrical body. Within this annular piece, a lubricating oil channel is formed that connects with the oil inlet on the cylindrical member.

**Sealing Elements**: Two seal rings are mounted—either on the cylindrical body or the annular component—positioned on opposite sides of the oil inlet along the axial direction.

**Bypass Channels**: Passages are incorporated to circumvent each of the two seal rings, allowing oil to flow around them.

# Oil Supply Structure for Planetary Gear Device

## Overview

The present oil supply structure is designed for application in a planetary gear device and addresses the need for reliable, controlled lubrication delivery to rotating components while minimizing leakage and pressure loss. The structure comprises several interrelated components that work in concert to achieve efficient oil transfer between stationary and rotating members.

## Tubular Body Configuration

The oil supply structure incorporates a planetary gear device that includes a tubular body configured to rotate integrally with the carrier that supports and holds the planetary gears. This tubular body serves as a critical conduit within the lubrication system, as it has a lubricating oil introduction port formed directly within its structure. This introduction port serves as the entry point through which lubricating oil is delivered into the tubular body for subsequent distribution to the planetary gear components requiring lubrication.

## Annular Body and Oil Passage

An annular body is arranged so as to slide against the outer or inner surface of the tubular body, establishing a rotational sliding interface between the two components. This annular body is formed with a lubricating oil supply passage that is configured to communicate with the lubricating oil introduction port of the tubular body. Through this arrangement, lubricating oil can be continuously supplied from the annular body—which may remain stationary or rotate at a different speed than the tubular body—into the rotating tubular body, thereby accommodating the relative rotational motion between the two members while maintaining an unbroken oil supply path.

## Seal Ring Arrangement

To prevent unwanted leakage of lubricating oil at the sliding interface between the tubular body and the annular body, a pair of seal rings is provided. These seal rings are attached to either the tubular body or the annular body and are positioned on both axial sides of the lubricating oil introduction port. This dual seal ring configuration effectively brackets the introduction port, creating a sealed zone that confines the lubricating oil to the intended flow path and inhibits its escape in either axial direction along the sliding surface.

## Bypass Passage Function

In addition to the sealing arrangement, bypass passages are incorporated into the structure so as to bypass each of the pair of seal rings individually. These bypass passages provide an alternative flow route around each seal ring, allowing a controlled, limited amount of lubricating oil to pass beyond the sealing points rather than being entirely blocked. This design feature helps to manage pressure differentials across the seal rings and can serve to lubricate the seal ring contact surfaces themselves, thereby reducing wear and extending the operational life of the sealing elements.

## Pressure Reduction Mechanisms

To further regulate the oil flow that passes through the bypass passages, a pair of pressure reduction mechanisms is provided. These mechanisms are positioned either between the lubricating oil introduction port and the respective seal rings, or alternatively on the outer side of the seal rings relative to the introduction port. Each pressure reduction mechanism functions to restrict and limit the flow of lubricating oil between the tubular body and the annular body, effectively throttling the leakage flow permitted by the bypass passages. By controlling the rate of oil flow at these locations, the pressure reduction mechanisms help maintain an appropriate pressure balance within the lubrication system, ensuring that sufficient oil pressure is preserved for the primary lubrication function while preventing excessive oil loss through the bypass routes.

## Summary

Collectively, this arrangement—comprising the rotating tubular body with its introduction port, the sliding annular body with its communicating supply passage, the paired seal rings flanking the introduction port, the bypass passages circumventing each seal ring, and the paired pressure reduction mechanisms regulating bypass flow—provides a robust and efficient means of supplying lubricating oil to the planetary gear device. This configuration balances the competing demands of secure sealing, controlled leakage for seal lubrication, and overall system pressure management, resulting in a lubrication structure well-suited to the dynamic operating conditions of planetary gear systems.

# Oil Supply Structure for Planetary Gear Device

## Technical Field

The present disclosure relates to an oil supply structure for a planetary gear device, and more particularly to a configuration for delivering lubricating oil to rotating components within planetary gear systems commonly used in automotive transmissions, industrial gearboxes, and other rotating machinery applications.

## Background

Planetary gear devices require consistent and reliable lubrication to rotating components such as planet gears, bearings, and other elements subject to relative rotational motion. Conventional oil supply structures often face challenges in delivering lubricating oil across the interface between stationary and rotating components without excessive leakage or pressure buildup that can lead to premature wear at sliding interfaces. There exists a need for an improved oil supply structure that can reliably deliver lubricating oil while minimizing these drawbacks.

## Summary of the Invention

The present oil supply structure for a planetary gear device comprises a tubular body and an annular body configured to interface with one another to facilitate the controlled delivery of lubricating oil to rotating components within the gear assembly.

### Tubular Body Configuration

The tubular body includes an introduction port formed therein, through which lubricating oil is introduced into the supply structure. This introduction port is positioned and configured to interface directly with a corresponding supply passage formed in the annular body, establishing a fluid communication pathway between the two components.

### Annular Body and Supply Passage

The annular body is configured with a supply passage that receives lubricating oil from the tubular body's introduction port. The annular body is arranged to rotate relative to the tubular body, or vice versa, such that the interface between the introduction port and the supply passage must accommodate relative rotational movement while maintaining fluid communication.

### Sealing Mechanism

To prevent leakage of lubricating oil at the sliding interface between the tubular body and the annular body, a pair of seal rings is provided. These seal rings are positioned on either side of the introduction port and supply passage interface, effectively bracketing the oil transfer region. The paired seal ring arrangement creates a sealed chamber around the interface point, containing the lubricating oil within a defined space and preventing unwanted migration of oil beyond the intended flow path.

### Bypass Passages and Pressure Reduction Mechanisms

Positioned around the seal rings are bypass passages and pressure reduction mechanisms that work in conjunction with the sealing structure to regulate the flow characteristics of the lubricating oil. These bypass passages provide alternative flow paths that can relieve excess pressure that may build up within the sealed chamber during operation. The pressure reduction mechanisms further modulate the oil flow, ensuring that pressure levels at the seal ring interfaces remain within acceptable ranges.

This arrangement of bypass passages and pressure reduction mechanisms serves multiple functions:

1. **Flow Limitation**: By providing controlled bypass routes, the structure limits the volume and rate of lubricating oil flow between the tubular body and annular body, preventing oversupply that could lead to inefficiency or oil loss.

2. **Pressure Regulation**: The pressure reduction mechanisms actively manage pressure differentials across the seal rings, reducing the mechanical stress placed on the seals during operation.

3. **Wear Mitigation**: By moderating pressure at the sliding interface between the tubular body and annular body, the structure significantly reduces the wear that would otherwise occur due to sustained high-pressure contact between rotating and stationary sealing surfaces.

## Advantages of the Configuration

This oil supply structure configuration offers several advantages over conventional designs:

- **Reliable Lubrication**: The direct interface between the introduction port and supply passage ensures that lubricating oil is consistently delivered to the rotating components of the planetary gear device, supporting proper lubrication under varying operating conditions.

- **Minimized Leakage**: The paired seal ring arrangement, combined with the bypass and pressure reduction features, substantially reduces the potential for lubricating oil to leak from the intended flow path, improving overall system efficiency and reducing oil consumption.

- **Reduced Wear at Sliding Interfaces**: By actively managing pressure at the critical sliding interface between the tubular body and annular body, the structure extends the operational lifespan of the seal rings and associated components, reducing maintenance requirements and improving long-term reliability.

- **Effective Flow Control**: The combination of bypass passages and pressure reduction mechanisms allows for precise control over lubricating oil flow, ensuring that the right amount of oil reaches the rotating components without excess that could lead to operational inefficiencies.

## Conclusion

The described oil supply structure represents an effective solution for delivering lubricating oil to rotating components within a planetary gear device. Through the strategic combination of a tubular body with an introduction port, an annular body with a corresponding supply passage, paired seal rings, and surrounding bypass passages with pressure reduction mechanisms, this configuration achieves reliable lubrication delivery while simultaneously addressing the critical concerns of leakage prevention and wear reduction at sliding interfaces. This structure is particularly well-suited for applications where planetary gear devices must operate under demanding conditions requiring consistent, controlled lubrication over extended service periods.

# The Global Oil Supply Chain: A Critical Lifeline

The oil supply represents one of the most complex and consequential logistics networks in the modern world, connecting extraction sites deep beneath deserts and ocean floors to gas stations, factories, and power plants across the globe. This intricate system involves exploration, drilling, refining, transportation, and distribution—each stage requiring massive infrastructure investment and precise coordination.

## From Ground to Global Markets

The journey begins with exploration teams identifying viable reserves, followed by the construction of drilling platforms, whether onshore rigs in places like Texas and Saudi Arabia or offshore platforms in the North Sea and Gulf of Mexico. Once extracted, crude oil travels through pipelines, tanker ships, and railways to reach refineries, where it's transformed into gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, and countless petrochemical products.

## Geopolitical Significance

Few commodities carry as much geopolitical weight as oil. Nations with abundant reserves, such as members of OPEC, wield significant influence over global energy prices and, by extension, economic stability worldwide. Supply disruptions—whether from conflicts, sanctions, natural disasters, or production decisions—can send shockwaves through markets, affecting everything from transportation costs to the price of everyday goods.

## Vulnerability and Resilience

The oil supply chain has repeatedly demonstrated both its fragility and resilience. Events like the 1973 oil embargo, the 1990 Gulf War, and more recent disruptions from geopolitical conflicts have exposed how quickly supply shortages can trigger economic turmoil. In response, many countries maintain strategic petroleum reserves as buffers against sudden interruptions, while others have diversified their energy sources to reduce dependency on any single supplier or region.

## The Path Forward

As the world grapples with climate change, the oil supply chain faces unprecedented pressure to evolve. While renewable energy sources are steadily gaining ground, oil remains deeply embedded in global infrastructure, transportation systems, and manufacturing processes. The transition away from fossil fuels will likely be gradual, requiring careful management of existing oil supply networks even as investment shifts toward sustainable alternatives.

Understanding the oil supply chain—its strengths, vulnerabilities, and the delicate balance of power it represents—remains essential for policymakers, businesses, and consumers navigating an increasingly interconnected and energy-dependent world.

a pair of seal rings disposed at axially spaced positions along the sliding interface between the rotating tubular body and the annular sliding body, the seal rings being configured to seal an annular oil supply chamber formed between the rotating tubular body and the annular sliding body, so as to prevent leakage of the lubricating oil supplied to the annular oil supply chamber;

**Claim 4:**

The oil supply structure for a planetary gear device according to claim 1, wherein the rotating tubular body includes a plurality of radial oil holes formed in a wall thereof, the radial oil holes providing fluid communication between the annular oil supply chamber and the internal oil passage of the rotating tubular body.

The oil supply structure for a planetary gear device according to claim 1, wherein the bypass passage extends radially through the annular sliding body and communicates with a drain passage formed in the housing, such that the diverted lubricating oil is returned to an oil reservoir after passing through the pressure reduction mechanism.

**Claim 7:**

The oil supply structure for a planetary gear device according to claim 1, wherein the pressure reduction mechanism includes a labyrinth passage formed along at least a portion of the bypass passage, the labyrinth passage being configured to progressively reduce the pressure of the lubricating oil as it flows therethrough.

# OIL SUPPLY STRUCTURE FOR AUTOMOTIVE TRANSMISSION

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present invention relates to an oil supply structure for automotive transmissions, and more particularly to an oil supply structure for lubricating and cooling rotating components such as planetary carriers, clutch packs, and bearing assemblies within an automatic transmission mechanism.

## BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION

In automotive transmissions, planetary gear sets and associated carrier assemblies rotate at varying speeds relative to the transmission case during operation. These rotating components require continuous lubrication and cooling to prevent excessive wear, heat generation, and premature failure of bearings, gears, and friction elements.

Conventional oil supply structures typically deliver lubricating oil from a stationary source, such as a transmission case or oil pump, to rotating components through a series of passages and seals. However, such conventional structures often suffer from several drawbacks. First, the pressure of the lubricating oil supplied to the rotating oil passages may be excessively high, resulting in oil supply amounts exceeding what is actually required for adequate lubrication, thereby causing unnecessary pumping losses and reduced fuel efficiency. Second, maintaining adequate sealing between stationary and rotating components while accommodating relative rotational movement presents ongoing design challenges. Third, existing structures often lack effective means for regulating oil pressure and flow rate in accordance with actual lubrication demands, particularly under varying rotational speed conditions.

Accordingly, there exists a need for an improved oil supply structure that can reliably deliver lubricating oil to rotating transmission components while regulating oil pressure to reduce excess supply, minimize pumping losses, and maintain robust sealing performance across a range of operating conditions.

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

According to an aspect of the present invention, an oil supply structure is provided for supplying lubricating oil to a rotating member, such as a carrier, of an automotive transmission. The oil supply structure comprises a tubular body configured to rotate together with the carrier, an annular body disposed radially outward of or adjacent to the tubular body and formed with a lubricating oil passage, one or more sealing rings interposed between the tubular body and the annular body to prevent oil leakage while permitting relative rotation, and a pressure reducing bypass mechanism configured to regulate the flow rate and pressure of the lubricating oil supplied through the oil passage.

In one embodiment, the tubular body includes a cylindrical portion press-fit onto or splined to the carrier such that the tubular body rotates integrally therewith. The tubular body defines therein a supply passage extending in an axial direction and communicating with a plurality of radial through-holes formed in a peripheral wall of the tubular body.

The annular body is disposed so as to surround an outer peripheral surface of the tubular body, forming therebetween an annular oil chamber that communicates with the radial through-holes of the tubular body. The annular body is further formed with the lubricating oil passage extending from the annular oil chamber to a supply port configured to introduce lubricating oil from a stationary oil source, such as an oil pump or a hydraulic control valve body of the transmission.

The sealing rings, which may comprise elastomeric O-rings, resin-based seal rings, or metallic piston rings, are disposed in annular grooves formed on the outer peripheral surface of the tubular body or on the inner peripheral surface of the annular body, positioned axially on opposite sides of the radial through-holes and the annular oil chamber, thereby sealing the annular oil chamber from adjacent regions and preventing leakage of lubricating oil along the interface between the tubular body and the annular body.

The pressure reducing bypass mechanism is provided in fluid communication with the lubricating oil passage or the annular oil chamber, and comprises a bypass passage, a valve body movably disposed within the bypass passage, and a biasing member, such as a coil spring, urging the valve body toward a closed position. When the pressure of the lubricating oil supplied to the oil supply structure exceeds a predetermined threshold value, the valve body is displaced against the biasing force of the biasing member to open the bypass passage, thereby discharging a portion of the lubricating oil to a low-pressure region, such as a drain passage or an oil pan, so as to reduce the pressure and flow rate of the lubricating oil ultimately supplied to the rotating member.

## BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS

FIG. 1 is a cross-sectional view illustrating an oil supply structure according to an embodiment of the present invention, showing the tubular body, the annular body, and the sealing rings in an assembled state.

FIG. 2 is an enlarged cross-sectional view illustrating the pressure reducing bypass mechanism of the oil supply structure of FIG. 1.

FIG. 3 is a cross-sectional view taken along line III-III of FIG. 1, illustrating the radial through-holes of the tubular body and the annular oil chamber.

FIG. 4 is a schematic view illustrating the flow of lubricating oil through the oil supply structure under a normal pressure condition.

FIG. 5 is a schematic view illustrating the flow of lubricating oil through the oil supply structure under a high pressure condition, wherein the pressure reducing bypass mechanism is in an open state.

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE PREFERRED EMBODIMENTS

Referring now to the drawings, wherein like reference numerals designate corresponding or identical elements throughout the several views, an oil supply structure 10 according to an embodiment of the present invention will be described.

### Overall Configuration

The oil supply structure 10 is provided within an automotive transmission (not shown in its entirety) for supplying lubricating oil to a carrier 1 of a planetary gear mechanism, the carrier 1 being rotatably supported within a transmission case. The oil supply structure 10 generally comprises a tubular body 20, an annular body 30, a plurality of sealing rings 40, and a pressure reducing bypass mechanism 50.

### Tubular Body

The tubular body 20 comprises a substantially cylindrical member having a first end portion 21 fixedly coupled to the carrier 1, for example, by spline engagement, press-fitting, or welding, such that the tubular body 20 rotates integrally with the carrier 1 about a rotational axis O. The tubular body 20 defines an internal supply passage 22 extending along the rotational axis O, the internal supply passage 22 being in fluid communication with an oil passage formed within the carrier 1 for ultimately delivering lubricating oil to bearings, thrust washers, and meshing gear portions of the planetary gear mechanism.

The tubular body 20 further includes a peripheral wall 23 formed with a plurality of radial through-holes 24 arranged circumferentially at predetermined intervals, the radial through-holes 24 extending from an outer peripheral surface 25 of the tubular body 20 to the internal supply passage 22, thereby permitting lubricating oil to flow from an exterior of the tubular body 20 into the internal supply passage 22 regardless of the rotational position of the tubular body 20.

### Annular Body

The annular body 30 is disposed radially outward of the tubular body 20 and is fixed relative to the transmission case, or alternatively relative to another stationary member, such that the annular body 30 does not rotate together with the tubular body 20. An inner peripheral surface 31 of the annular body 30 is disposed in opposing relation to the outer peripheral surface 25 of the tubular body 20, with a predetermined radial clearance defined therebetween so as to permit relative rotational sliding.

The annular body 30 is formed with a lubricating oil passage 32 extending from a supply port 33, which is configured to receive pressurized lubricating oil from an oil pump or a hydraulic control valve body of the transmission, to an annular oil chamber 34 defined circumferentially about the outer peripheral surface 25 of the tubular body 20 between the inner peripheral surface 31 of the annular body 30 and the outer peripheral surface 25 of the tubular body 20. The annular oil chamber 34 is positioned so as to communicate with the radial through-holes 24 of the tubular body 20 regardless of the rotational angle of the tubular body 20, thereby ensuring continuous oil supply during rotation.

### Sealing Rings

A plurality of sealing rings 40, in the illustrated embodiment a first sealing ring 41 and a second sealing ring 42, are disposed within annular grooves 26 formed in the outer peripheral surface 25 of the tubular body 20, the annular grooves 26 being positioned axially on opposite sides of the radial through-holes 24. The first sealing ring 41 and the second sealing ring 42 are each configured to sealingly engage the inner peripheral surface 31 of the annular body 30, thereby defining and sealing the annular oil chamber 34 axially therebetween and preventing leakage of lubricating oil from the annular oil chamber 34 toward adjacent regions of the transmission.

In an alternative embodiment, the sealing rings 40 may be disposed within annular grooves formed in the inner peripheral surface 31 of the annular body 30, in sealing engagement with the outer peripheral surface 25 of the tubular body 20, without departing from the scope of the present invention. The sealing rings 40 may be formed of a resin material having a low coefficient of friction, such as polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), or may alternatively comprise elastomeric O-rings or metallic seal rings, depending on the operating temperature, pressure, and rotational speed requirements of the particular application.

### Pressure Reducing Bypass Mechanism

The pressure reducing bypass mechanism 50 is provided in the annular body 30 and is configured to regulate the pressure and flow rate of the lubricating oil supplied to the annular oil chamber 34. The pressure reducing bypass mechanism 50 comprises a bypass passage 51 branching from the lubricating oil passage 32 upstream of the annular oil chamber 34, a valve body 52 slidably disposed within a valve bore 53 formed in the annular body 30 and communicating with the bypass passage 51, and a biasing member 54, such as a coil spring, disposed within the valve bore 53 and configured to urge the valve body 52 toward a closed position in which the bypass passage 51 is blocked by the valve body 52.

The valve body 52 includes a pressure receiving surface 55 exposed to the pressure of the lubricating oil within the lubricating oil passage 32, such that when the oil pressure within the lubricating oil passage 32 exceeds a predetermined threshold value corresponding to a set force of the biasing member 54, the valve body 52 is displaced against the biasing force of the biasing member 54 to an open position, thereby opening the bypass passage 51 and permitting a portion of the lubricating oil to be discharged to a low-pressure region 56, such as a drain passage communicating with an oil pan of the transmission.

By this configuration, when the oil pump discharge pressure is relatively high, such as during high engine speed operation, the pressure reducing bypass mechanism 50 automatically diverts excess lubricating oil away from the annular oil chamber 34 and the tubular body 20, thereby preventing an excessive amount of lubricating oil from being supplied to the carrier 1 and reducing unnecessary pumping losses. Conversely, when the oil pump discharge pressure is relatively low, such as during idle or low engine speed operation, the biasing member 54 maintains the valve body 52 in the closed position, such that substantially all of the lubricating oil supplied through the lubricating oil passage 32 is directed to the annular oil chamber 34 and thence to the carrier 1, ensuring adequate lubrication under such conditions.
